passage: Anirban, come sit with me. I'm your Jeevan Kaka, and I heard your friends telling scary tales about the police. I was scared once too. A boy in my class, Manik, swore a constable would lock me up for stepping off the pavement, and for weeks I crossed the road to avoid the one at our corner. Then I asked my father. He said, "Their job is to help, especially children. If you are ever lost, go to them." At the Durga Puja pandal I let go of his hand. My knees shook. I found a constable with a whistle, told him my name and my father's, and he gave me water and called my father over the loudspeaker. Ask your Baba what police really do.

qa.q: Where did Jeevan let go of his father's hand?
qa.a: He let go of it at the Durga Puja pandal.

qa.q: Why did young Jeevan cross the road to avoid the constable at the corner?
qa.a: He was frightened by Manik's scary tale and thought the constable would lock him up.

qa.q: What could Anirban do about the scary stories from friends?
qa.a: Anirban can ask Baba what police really do, as Jeevan asked his father.

qa.q: How did the constable seem to see the lost boy?
qa.a: As a child who needed help. He gave the boy water and called his father over the loudspeaker.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling fear built from friends' stories about police, asking his father, and then being helped by a constable.

passage:
Tuesday: At lunch Minakshi whispered, "If you're naughty, the police put you in a jail with rats. My cousin said." Walking home past the police station, Kavitha kept her eyes on her shoes, her heart beating fast.
Wednesday: At dinner she asked Amma, "Do police take away naughty children?" Amma put down her roti. "No, kanna. Police help people. If you're lost, or someone hurts you, they help. Who told you that?" Kavitha explained. Amma laughed gently. "Minakshi's cousin likes stories."
Friday: On the class trip to the police station, Sub-Inspector Mary showed them the wireless set and the helpline number painted on the wall. Minakshi hid behind Kavitha at first, but the officer let them both try on her cap. Walking out, Kavitha waved at the constable at the gate. He waved back.

qa.q: What did Minakshi say police do to naughty children?
qa.a: Put them in a jail with rats.

qa.q: How did Kavitha feel walking past the police station on Tuesday?
qa.a: Nervous; she kept her eyes on her shoes and her heart beat fast.

qa.q: What helped Kavitha replace the scary story with facts?
qa.a: Asking Amma at dinner, and then visiting the police station on the class trip.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt on the trip?
qa.a: Scared at first, hiding behind Kavitha, then more at ease after trying on the cap.

grounding: A girl made nervous by friends' scary stories about police asks her parent and learns that a good officer helps children.

passage: Devika, your friends say the police will catch you for picking the neighbour's jamun? Ha! Let your Neelam Nani tell you. When I was your age, my cousins told me the thanedar kept naughty children in a cage behind the police chowki. Every time I saw a khaki uniform on the village road, I ran and hid in the sugarcane. Then one monsoon our buffalo was stolen. Bapu went to the chowki, and I went with him, shaking. The thanedar gave me a glass of water and listened to Bapu, and three days later he rode into our courtyard leading our buffalo by the rope. I asked him, "Where is the cage?" He laughed till his cap fell off. "There is no cage for children, beti. We are here to help you." So, Devika, ask your Amma what police really do.

qa.q: What did the thanedar bring back three days later?
How did young Neelam feel whenever she saw a khaki uniform?
qa.a: Scared, so she ran and hid in the sugarcane.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Nani's story?
qa.a: Going with Bapu to the chowki and seeing the thanedar help get their buffalo back.

qa.q: How did the thanedar react to the question about the cage?
qa.a: He laughed till his cap fell off and explained that police are there to help children.

grounding: A grandmother recalls how scary stories made her fear the police until she saw an officer help her family.
